chapters.title: File Organization
chapters.subtitle: Methods of storing data in files. Determines how records are physically arranged on storage media.

blocks.text: Types of File Organization

items: Serial
Sequential
Random
Simplest method of file organization
Data is stored as it comes
Data is ALWAYS appended (added to the end of the file)
Follows chronological order

blocks.text: Examples: Text files, transaction records, log files

items: Data is stored based on key field sequentially
Key fields have to be unique AND in order

blocks.text: HITRATE: The number of files that can be accessed at one moment.

items: Has high hitrate → Can apply batch processing
Adding new data → Re-arrange memory → Time and power-consuming process

blocks.text: Important: Sequential files have to be in order. Inserting data in the middle means moving ALL data after the insertion point by one position.
Adding new data requires re-arranging memory, which is time and power-consuming.

items: Data is stored randomly
Records are stored at an address generated by a hashing algorithm applied to the key field
HITRATE: Has a low hitrate → Few records can be accessed at a time

blocks.text: Examples: ATMs, files with usernames and passwords
Collision
A collision occurs when one data index is assigned the same memory address as another index.
Reasons for a Collision

items: A record is already written at the address given by the hashing algorithm
Two or more records are matched to the same hash address
The number of key fields is greater than the number of memory addresses

blocks.text: Closed Hashing
Move line by line to find the first available free space.
Open Hashing (Chaining)
Also known as Chaining. Create a separate linked list of all elements that are in collision.
Overflow Area
A separate memory area assigned for elements in collision.
1. Sequential Access
Move element by element to access records. Used with Serial and Sequential file organizations.
2. Direct Access
Apply a hashing algorithm to the key field. An address is generated and the system directly accesses the required record. FASTEST method to access data.
If the record is not available, linearly move from the hash address until:

items: Record is found
Empty space is found
Last address is reached

blocks.text: Used with: Sequential and Random file organizations

chapters.title: Real Numbers
chapters.subtitle: Binary representation of decimals using mantissa and exponent.

blocks.text: Overview
Real numbers can be represented in binary using a few key techniques:

items: Converting denary values to binary
Handling repeating decimals
Using two's complement for signed values
Storing values using mantissa and exponent form

blocks.text: To convert a real number to binary:

items: Convert the integer part to binary
Multiply the fractional part by 2
Record the integer part as the next binary bit
Repeat until the fractional part becomes 0 or a repeating cycle is detected

blocks.text: The integer part is 7: 7 in binary = 111
The fractional part is 0.25:
Result: 7.25 = 111.01
10 in binary = 1010. Fractional part: 0.7
Therefore: 10.7 ≈ 1010.101100
The repeating section is ignored after one cycle, so the answer is shown as a recurring binary pattern.
Two's complement is used to represent signed numbers in binary, especially when handling floating-point mantissas.
Method 1: Flip & Add 1

items: Flip every bit
+ 1

blocks.text: Method 2: Place-Value Table (method used in the examples below)
Same as normal binary place values, except the leftmost (Most Significant) bit is negative.
Convert -47 to 8-bit Two's Complement
Computers cannot store decimals directly, so real numbers are stored as a mantissa and an exponent. This is the method used in floating-point representation.
Mantissa
The mantissa contains the significant digits of the number.

items: It represents the precision of the value
More digits usually means greater precision

blocks.text: Example: 5.25 and 5.2575, the second value has more precision because it contains more digits after the decimal point.
Exponent

items: It represents the range of the number
It is related to the position of the decimal point

blocks.text: Convert +47.25 (12-bit Mantissa, 5-bit Exponent)
First, convert 47.25 to binary:
This gives: 47.25 = 101111.01 in binary
Final Mantissa
Move the decimal point so it is just before the first 1:
The decimal point moves 6 places to the left, so the exponent is 6.
Final Exponent
mantissa = 0.10111101000  and  exponent = 6
Why it is needed
Floating-point numbers cannot always be stored exactly because the computer has a limited number of bits.

items: A stored value is usually slightly higher or lower than the real value
This is called rounding error

blocks.text: Examples:
Normalized form
Normalization reduces error and makes the representation more accurate. The important rule is that the first two bits of the mantissa cannot be the same:
Normalization is basically the process of adjusting the decimal point so the number is stored in the most efficient and accurate format.
Why normalization matters

items: Keeps the mantissa accurate
Avoids losing bits
Removes multiple representations of the same number
Helps represent very large and very small numbers more reliably

blocks.text: Before normalization
This starts with 00, which is not normalized.
Correct position for the decimal point
Move the decimal point to the left until the mantissa begins with 01 or 10, this is the normalized form.
Exponent example
This value is 24 in binary, so the exponent is adjusted by the number of places the decimal point moved.
Final rule

items: Move the decimal point between the first two bits of the mantissa
Adjust the exponent by the same number of places moved
If you move left, exponent increases
If you move right, exponent decreases
Denary numbers are converted to binary by splitting integer and fractional parts
Repeating decimals are stopped after one cycle
Two's complement is used for signed integer values
Mantissa and exponent store real numbers in a compact form
Normalization keeps the number accurate and avoids wasted or repeated representations

chapters.title: User Defined Data Types
chapters.subtitle: Custom data types to reduce code complexity when built-in types are insufficient.

blocks.text: A user created datatype that can be customized.

items: Good for when software does not provide a datatype
Reduces code complexity

blocks.text: Non-Composite
Non Composite: Can hold ONE value, does NOT depend on any other datatypes.

items: Built-in: STRING, CHAR, INTEGER, REAL, BOOLEAN
User Defined: Enumerated, Pointer

blocks.text: A list that is ALWAYS in order / an ordered list of elements.

TYPE Day = (Mon,Tue,Wed,Thu,Fri,Sat,Sun)

DECLARE MyDay : Day
MyDay <-- Tue
REMEMBER: string values are NOT enclosed in quotes or commas here.
Pointers point to memory locations.
Let's say the pointer is at memory location 101 and is called Name:

items: OUTPUT Name → outputs Ayan
OUTPUT ^Name → outputs 101 (memory location / address)
OUTPUT Name^ → outputs Ayan (the value at that location)

blocks.text: When a pointer points toward a memory location (^Name). When a pointer points toward a value and not a memory location (Name^).
TYPE MyPointer = ^INTEGER
Makes a pointer that points to an integer.
Composite
Composite: Holds multiple values, same or different.

items: Built-in: Array, Linked List, Stack, Queue
User Defined: Record, CLASS, SET

blocks.text: Collection of different datatypes represented as one identifier.

TYPE Student
    DECLARE Surname : STRING
    DECLARE Age : INTEGER
    DECLARE Mark : REAL
ENDTYPE

DECLARE MyStudent : Student
MyStudent.Surname <-- "Esa"
MyStudent.Age <-- 15
MyStudent.Mark <-- 90.5
A collection of attributes and methods having different relationships applied to them.

items: Used in Object Oriented Programming (OOP)
We'll cover this later in Classes

blocks.text: Unordered list of elements to which we apply different mathematical operations.

TYPE MySet = SET OF INTEGER

DEFINE MyNumbers (1, 2, 3, 4) : MySet
MySet is declared as a set that can hold integers, and MyNumbers is defined as a MySet containing the values 1, 2, 3 and 4.
Example: A, "A"

flashcards.definition: The simplest method of file organization. Data is stored as it comes in and is ALWAYS appended (added) to the end of the file, following chronological order.
flashcards.details: No ordering or sorting is applied — new records simply go after the last record written.
flashcards.example: Examples: text files, transaction records, log files

questions.q: Which is the simplest method of file organization?
questions.a: Serial

questions.q: In serial file organization, where is new data added?
questions.a: Always appended to the end of the file

questions.q: What order does serial file organization follow?
questions.a: Chronological order

questions.q: Give two examples of files that use serial organization.
questions.a: Log files and transaction records (also text files)

flashcards.definition: Data is stored based on the key field sequentially — key fields have to be unique AND in order.
flashcards.details: Has a HIGH hitrate, so batch processing can be applied. Adding new data means re-arranging memory, because every record after the insertion point must move by one position — a time and power-consuming process.
flashcards.example: Primary keys 208, 201, 205 are physically stored in key field order: 201, 205, 208.

questions.q: In sequential file organization, what must be true about key fields?
questions.a: They must be unique AND in order

questions.q: Which file organization has a high hitrate and suits batch processing?
questions.a: Sequential

questions.q: Why is inserting into a sequential file expensive?
questions.a: All data after the insertion point must be moved to keep the order — re-arranging memory is time and power-consuming

flashcards.definition: Records are stored randomly, at an address generated by applying a hashing algorithm to the key field.
flashcards.details: Has a LOW hitrate — few records can be accessed at a time.
flashcards.example: Examples: ATMs, files with usernames and passwords

questions.q: How is a record's storage address calculated in random file organization?
questions.a: By applying a hashing algorithm to the key field

questions.q: What kind of hitrate does random file organization have?
questions.a: A low hitrate (few records can be accessed at a time)

questions.q: Give an example of where random file organization is used.
questions.a: ATMs (also files with usernames and passwords)

flashcards.definition: The number of files (records) that can be accessed at one moment.
flashcards.details: Sequential file organization has a HIGH hitrate. Random file organization has a LOW hitrate.

questions.q: What does hitrate measure?
questions.a: The number of files that can be accessed at one moment

questions.q: Which has the higher hitrate: sequential or random file organization?
questions.a: Sequential

flashcards.definition: A collision occurs when one data index is assigned the same memory address as another index.
flashcards.details: Reasons for a collision: 1) A record is already written at the address given by the hashing algorithm. 2) Two or more records are matched to the same hash address. 3) The number of key fields is greater than the number of memory addresses.

questions.q: What is a collision?
questions.a: When one data index is assigned the same memory address as another index

questions.q: Name one reason why a collision can occur.
questions.a: A record is already written at the address, two or more records match to the same hash address, or there are more key fields than memory addresses

flashcards.definition: Three ways to handle collisions: closed hashing, open hashing (chaining) and overflow areas.
flashcards.details: Closed hashing: move line by line to find the first available free space. Open hashing (chaining): create a separate linked list of all elements that are in collision. Overflow area: a separate memory area assigned for elements in collision.

questions.q: Which collision solution moves line by line to find the first free space?
questions.a: Closed hashing

questions.q: What is open hashing also known as?
questions.a: Chaining

questions.q: What data structure does open hashing use for colliding elements?
questions.a: A linked list

questions.q: What is an overflow area?
questions.a: A separate memory area assigned for elements in collision

flashcards.definition: Move element by element through the file to access records. Used with Serial and Sequential file organizations.

questions.q: Which file organizations use sequential access?
questions.a: Serial and Sequential

questions.q: How does sequential access reach a record?
questions.a: By moving element by element

flashcards.definition: Apply a hashing algorithm to the key field — the generated address lets the system access the required record directly. It is the FASTEST method to access data.
flashcards.details: If the record is not at the hash address, move linearly from it until: the record is found, an empty space is found, or the last address is reached. Used with Sequential and Random file organizations.

questions.q: What is the fastest method to access data?
questions.a: Direct access

questions.q: When does the linear search from the hash address stop?
questions.a: When the record is found, an empty space is found, or the last address is reached

questions.q: Which file organizations use direct access?
questions.a: Sequential and Random

flashcards.definition: Convert the integer part to binary normally, then convert the fractional part by repeatedly multiplying by 2 and recording the integer part of each result.
flashcards.details: Steps: 1) Convert the integer part to binary. 2) Multiply the fractional part by 2. 3) Record the integer part as the next binary bit. 4) Repeat until the fractional part becomes 0 or a repeating cycle is detected.

questions.q: How do you convert the fractional part of a denary number to binary?
questions.a: Multiply it by 2 repeatedly and record the integer part each time

questions.q: What is 7.25 in binary?
When do you stop multiplying the fraction by 2?
questions.a: When the fractional part becomes 0 or a repeating cycle is detected

flashcards.definition: Some denary fractions never reach 0 when multiplied by 2 — they produce a repeating cycle of bits instead.
flashcards.details: The repeating section is ignored after one cycle, so the answer is shown as a recurring binary pattern.

questions.q: What happens to a fraction like 0.7 in binary?
questions.a: It produces a repeating cycle of bits (recurring binary pattern)

questions.q: 10.7 in binary is approximately…?
questions.a: 1010.101100 (repeating)

flashcards.definition: A method to represent signed numbers in binary. The Most Significant Bit (MSB) carries a negative place value.
flashcards.details: Method 1 — Flip & Add 1: flip every bit, then add 1. Method 2 — Place-value table: same as normal binary place values, except the leftmost (most significant) bit is negative.

questions.q: How do you negate a binary number using flip & add 1?
questions.a: Flip every bit, then add 1

questions.q: In a two's complement place-value table, what is special about the MSB?
questions.a: It is negative (e.g. -128 in 8 bits)

questions.q: Write -47 as an 8-bit two's complement number.

flashcards.definition: The part of a floating-point number that contains the significant digits. It represents the precision of the value.
flashcards.details: More digits (usually after the decimal point) means greater precision.
flashcards.example: 5.2575 has more precision than 5.25 because it contains more digits after the decimal point.

questions.q: What does the mantissa represent?
questions.a: The significant digits of the number — its precision

questions.q: Which has greater precision: 5.25 or 5.2575?

flashcards.definition: The part of a floating-point number that represents the range of the number. It is related to the position of the decimal point.

questions.q: What does the exponent represent?
questions.a: The range of the number (it relates to the position of the decimal point)

flashcards.definition: Computers cannot store decimals directly, so real numbers are stored as a mantissa and an exponent — the method used in floating-point representation.
flashcards.example: 47.25 = 101111.01 in binary. Move the point 6 places left: mantissa = 0.10111101000 (12-bit) and exponent = 6 (00110 in 5-bit).

questions.q: Why are real numbers stored as mantissa and exponent?
questions.a: Because computers cannot store decimals directly

questions.q: 47.25 is 101111.01 in binary. What is the exponent after moving the binary point?
questions.a: 6 (the point moves 6 places to the left)

flashcards.definition: Adjusting the decimal point so a floating-point number is stored in the most efficient and accurate format. The first two bits of the mantissa cannot be the same (01 and 10 are valid; 00 and 11 are not).
flashcards.details: If you move the decimal point LEFT, the exponent INCREASES. If you move it RIGHT, the exponent DECREASES. Benefits: keeps the mantissa accurate, avoids losing bits, removes multiple representations of the same number, and helps represent very large and very small numbers more reliably.

questions.q: What is the normalization rule for the first two bits of the mantissa?
questions.a: They cannot be the same — 01 and 10 are valid, 00 and 11 are not

questions.q: If you move the decimal point left, what happens to the exponent?
questions.a: It increases

questions.q: Give two reasons why we normalize.
questions.a: To reduce error / keep the mantissa accurate, and to remove multiple representations of the same number

flashcards.definition: Because the computer has a limited number of bits, a stored value is usually slightly higher or lower than the real value — this difference is called the rounding error.

questions.q: What is a rounding error?
questions.a: The difference between a stored value and the real value, caused by the limited number of bits

questions.q: 1/3 = 0.333333… illustrates which problem of storing real numbers?
questions.a: Rounding error (values cannot always be stored exactly)

flashcards.definition: A user-created datatype that can be customized. Good for when software does not provide a datatype, and it reduces code complexity.

questions.q: Why would you create a user-defined data type?
questions.a: When software does not provide a suitable datatype, and to reduce code complexity

flashcards.definition: A data type that can hold ONE value and does NOT depend on any other datatypes.
flashcards.details: Built-in: STRING, CHAR, INTEGER, REAL, BOOLEAN. User-defined: Enumerated, Pointer.

questions.q: How many values can a non-composite data type hold?
questions.a: One

questions.q: Name the two user-defined non-composite data types.
questions.a: Enumerated and Pointer

questions.q: Is INTEGER composite or non-composite?
questions.a: Non-composite (it holds one value)

flashcards.definition: A data type that holds multiple values, of the same or different types.
flashcards.details: Built-in: Array, Linked List, Stack, Queue. User-defined: Record, CLASS, SET.

questions.q: What is a composite data type?
questions.a: A data type that holds multiple values, same or different

questions.q: Name the three user-defined composite data types.
questions.a: Record, CLASS and SET

questions.q: Is a Stack composite or non-composite?
questions.a: Composite (it holds multiple values)

flashcards.definition: A list that is ALWAYS in order — an ordered list of elements.
flashcards.details: REMEMBER: enumerated values are NOT enclosed in quotes or commas.
flashcards.example:
TYPE Day = (Mon,Tue,Wed,Thu,Fri,Sat,Sun)

DECLARE MyDay : Day
MyDay <-- Tue

questions.q: What is an enumerated data type?
questions.a: An ordered list of elements

questions.q: How are values written in an enumerated type?
questions.a: Without quotes or commas, inside brackets

questions.q: Which user-defined type suits the days of the week?
questions.a: Enumerated

flashcards.definition: Pointers point to memory locations.
flashcards.details: ^Name refers to the memory location (address). Name^ refers to the value at that location.
flashcards.example: TYPE MyPointer = ^INTEGER — makes a pointer that points to an integer.

questions.q: What does a pointer point to?
questions.a: A memory location

questions.q: What does OUTPUT ^Name give?
questions.a: The memory location (address), e.g. 101

questions.q: What does OUTPUT Name^ give?
questions.a: The value at that memory location, e.g. Ayan

questions.q: How do you declare a pointer to an integer?
questions.a: TYPE MyPointer = ^INTEGER

flashcards.definition: A collection of different datatypes represented as one identifier.
flashcards.example:
TYPE Student
    DECLARE Surname : STRING
    DECLARE Age : INTEGER
    DECLARE Mark : REAL
ENDTYPE

DECLARE MyStudent : Student
MyStudent.Surname <-- "Esa"

questions.q: What is a record?
questions.a: A collection of different datatypes represented as one identifier

questions.q: How do you access a record's field?
questions.a: Using dot notation, e.g. MyStudent.Surname

flashcards.definition: A collection of attributes and methods having different relationships applied to them. Used in Object Oriented Programming (OOP).

questions.q: What is a class?
questions.a: A collection of attributes and methods having different relationships applied to them

questions.q: Which programming paradigm uses classes?
questions.a: Object Oriented Programming (OOP)

flashcards.definition: An unordered list of elements to which we apply different mathematical operations (e.g. union, intersection).
flashcards.example:
TYPE MySet = SET OF INTEGER

DEFINE MyNumbers (1, 2, 3, 4) : MySet

questions.q: What is a set?
questions.a: An unordered list of elements to which we apply mathematical operations

questions.q: How do you declare a set of integers called MySet?
questions.a: TYPE MySet = SET OF INTEGER

questions.q: How do you define MyNumbers as the set (1, 2, 3, 4) of type MySet?
questions.a: DEFINE MyNumbers (1, 2, 3, 4) : MySet

quiz.q: Which file organization stores data exactly as it arrives, always appending to the end of the file?
quiz.exp: Serial is the simplest method: data is stored as it comes, always appended, in chronological order.

quiz.q: In sequential file organization, key fields must be…
quiz.exp: Sequential stores records by key field sequentially, so keys must be unique AND in order (e.g. 201, 205, 208).

quiz.q: What does hitrate measure?
opts: Number of files on the disk
Number of files that can be accessed at one moment
quiz.exp: Hitrate is the number of files that can be accessed at one moment. Sequential has a high hitrate; random has a low one.

quiz.q: Which file organization calculates a record's address by applying a hashing algorithm to the key field?
quiz.exp: In random file organization, records are stored at an address generated by a hashing algorithm applied to the key field.

quiz.q: When does a collision occur?
opts: When two files have the same name
When the hashing algorithm fails to run
When one data index is assigned the same memory address as another
quiz.exp: A collision happens when one data index is assigned the same memory address as another — e.g. a record is already at the hash address, two records hash to the same address, or there are more key fields than memory addresses.

quiz.q: Which collision solution creates a linked list of all colliding elements?
quiz.exp: Open hashing is also known as chaining — a separate linked list holds all elements that are in collision.

quiz.q: Which collision solution moves line by line to find the first available free space?
quiz.exp: Closed hashing moves line by line from the hash address until a free space is found.

quiz.q: What is the FASTEST method to access data?
quiz.exp: Direct access applies a hashing algorithm to the key field and jumps straight to the record's address — the fastest method.

quiz.q: Sequential access is used with which file organizations?
quiz.exp: Sequential access moves element by element and is used with Serial and Sequential organizations; direct access is used with Sequential and Random.

quiz.q: In direct access, if the record is not at the hash address, you move linearly until…
opts: The record is found, an empty space is found, or the last address is reached
quiz.exp: The linear search stops when the record is found, an empty space is found, or the last address is reached.

quiz.q: To convert a denary fraction to binary, you repeatedly…
opts: Multiply by 2 and record the integer part
Divide by 2 and record the remainder
Multiply by 10 and record the result
quiz.exp: Multiply the fractional part by 2, record the integer part as the next bit, and repeat until the fraction is 0 or a cycle repeats.

quiz.q: What is 7.25 in binary?
10.7 in binary is approximately…
quiz.exp: 0.7 never reaches 0 — the bits repeat (…101100101100…), so the answer is shown as a recurring binary pattern.

quiz.q: Using flip & add 1, how do you negate a binary number?
quiz.exp: Two's complement negation: flip ALL bits, then add 1.

quiz.q: What is -47 in 8-bit two's complement?
quiz.exp: Using the place-value table with a negative MSB: -128 + 64 + 16 + 1 = -47 → 11010001.

quiz.q: The mantissa of a floating-point number represents its…
quiz.exp: The mantissa holds the significant digits and represents precision — more digits means greater precision.

quiz.q: The exponent of a floating-point number represents its…
quiz.exp: The exponent relates to the position of the decimal point and represents the range of the number.

quiz.q: A normalized mantissa must begin with…
quiz.exp: The first two bits of the mantissa cannot be the same: 01 and 10 are valid; 00 and 11 are not normalized.

quiz.q: If you move the binary point LEFT while normalizing, the exponent…
quiz.exp: Move left → exponent increases; move right → exponent decreases.

quiz.q: 47.25 = 101111.01 in binary. After normalization, the exponent is…
quiz.exp: The point moves 6 places left to give 0.10111101000, so the exponent is 6.
With a limited number of bits, the stored value is slightly higher or lower than the real value — a rounding error.

quiz.q: A non-composite data type can hold…
quiz.exp: Non-composite types hold ONE value and do not depend on any other datatype.

quiz.q: Which of these is a user-defined NON-composite data type?
quiz.exp: User-defined non-composite types are Enumerated and Pointer; Record, CLASS and SET are composite.

quiz.q: Which of these is a user-defined COMPOSITE data type?
quiz.exp: User-defined composite types are Record, CLASS and SET — they hold multiple values.

quiz.q: An enumerated data type is…
opts: A collection of attributes and methods
quiz.exp: Enumerated types are lists that are ALWAYS in order, e.g. TYPE Day = (Mon,Tue,Wed,Thu,Fri,Sat,Sun).

quiz.q: In pseudocode, OUTPUT ^Name gives…
quiz.exp: ^Name points toward the memory location (e.g. 101); Name^ points toward the value (e.g. Ayan).

quiz.q: In pseudocode, OUTPUT Name^ gives…
opts: The value stored at that memory location
quiz.exp: Name^ dereferences the pointer — it gives the value at the memory location.

quiz.q: A record is…
opts: A collection of different datatypes represented as one identifier
quiz.exp: A record groups different datatypes (e.g. STRING, INTEGER, REAL) under one identifier, accessed with dot notation.

quiz.q: A class is a collection of…
opts: Attributes and methods having relationships applied to them
quiz.exp: A class holds attributes and methods with different relationships, and is used in Object Oriented Programming.

quiz.q: How do you declare a set that can hold integers, called MySet?
quiz.exp: TYPE MySet = SET OF INTEGER declares MySet as a set of integers.

quiz.q: Which command defines MyNumbers as the set (1, 2, 3, 4) of type MySet?
quiz.exp: DEFINE MyNumbers (1, 2, 3, 4) : MySet defines MyNumbers as a MySet containing 1, 2, 3 and 4.
